items.title: Eddie Jones retains his passion and divisive power heading into England reunion
items.desc:
Japan head coach was criticised for discarding players harshly during his Red Rose tenure but that tough love has paid off for some

To listen to Eddie Jones chewing the fat on assorted podcasts this week is to admire the enduring thickness of his coaching skin. The old crocodile smile is still intact too, along with his sense of humour after an interaction in a lift with a fan after his Japan side’s 28-21 weekend defeat in Cardiff. As Jones later confided: “This Welsh bloke came up to me and said: ‘You almost look human with your glasses on.’”

Next up is a reunion with a few former friends – and foes – at Twickenham. While it is now almost four years since Jones was sacked by the Rugby Football Union, there remain mixed emotions on both sides. Those relieved to see him go in late 2022 will certainly not be too brokenhearted if there is a similar outcome to the last time a Jones-coached Japan came to Allianz Stadium two years ago and lost 59-14.

items.title: Rugby centre Henry Slade and his father look back: ‘I’d seen my dad live with diabetes, so my diagnosis wasn’t as upsetting as it might have been’
items.desc:
The England player on finding out he had type 1, the wonder of Jelly Babies, and the sacrifices his parents made for him

Born in Plymouth, Devon, in 1993, Henry Slade is a centre for Exeter Chiefs and England. He came up through the Exeter Chiefs academy, making his senior debut for the club in 2012, and has since earned more than 75 caps for England. He lifted the Champions Cup and won the Premiership title and the Six Nations in successive weekends in 2020. At 18, he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes – a condition his father, John, also lives with – and he has since launched the Tackle Diabetes campaign, in partnership with the pharmaceutical company Sanofi, to raise awareness of the signs and symptoms of the disease and the value of early detection. He lives near Exeter with his wife and three daughters. For more information about early detection, visit testfortype1.com

items.title: France have spent years trying to beat the Boks but belief and bodies are fading
items.desc:
Injury crisis makes the job harder for Fabien Galthié whose side have beaten South Africa once in their past 10 meetings

The final of this inaugural Nations Championship is two weeks away, but regardless of who makes it through to the last match at Twickenham there’s an irresistible sense that the two best teams from either side of the competition will go head-to-head at the Stade de France this Friday night. France, back-to-back Six Nations champions, play South Africa, back-to-back world champions, and the one team that the French – and anyone else with dreams of becoming the world’s best team – need to find a way to beat in the 12 months before the Springboks take a run at winning a third consecutive World Cup.

France have been looking for one of those for a long time now. This is not an even-sided rivalry. South Africa have won nine of the 10 games the two teams have played in the past 15 years, including the last five in Paris. England, Ireland, even Wales all have better head-to-head records against the Springboks in that same stretch of time. France’s one win was in Marseille in 2022, and whatever good it did them was undone a year later when the Springboks knocked them out of their home World Cup in the quarter-finals.

items.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
items.desc:
From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible

The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “war minus the shooting”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday?

Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart the domestic rugby set-up in Wales; and the growing appeal of football. Until Saturday, Welsh sports fans looking for a winning finish were better off watching the darts champion Gerwyn “The Iceman” Price than Steve Tandy’s rugby team.

items.title: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps
items.desc:
After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways

They still talk about the last – and only – time the All Blacks have contrived to lose twice in succession to England. Back in 2002-03, as now, there was a Rugby World Cup looming in Australia and New Zealand had no shortage of quality players. “There is so much talent in New Zealand that, if they don’t win the World Cup, there should be an inquiry,” opined Steve Hansen, Wales’s head coach at the time, ahead of England’s fateful visit to Wellington in the summer of 2003.

There’s a fresh inquiry under way now even before the All Blacks trot out of the Twickenham tunnel this weekend for the 48th meeting between the two nations. While Saturday’s 35-28 defeat to Wales ended a 73-year wait from a home perspective it has inevitably precipitated plenty of dark muttering back in the land of the long flat white.

items.title: France cling on for furious victory against South Africa after Dupont sizzles
items.desc:
• France 21-19 South Africa

  • Scrum-half key in thriller full of twists and turns

The French had been waiting 21 years to see their team beat the Springboks at the Stade de France. In that time the team turned through successive generations and multiple iterations, risen, fallen and risen again. Now, at last, they have done it. Only by two, 21-19, and hell, they were hanging on by the fingertips for the final 30 minutes, but they have, at last, beaten the best team in the world in their national stadium. And after all that they did it with a team that had barely won a lineout, lost almost every scrum and which was missing a host of players.

What they did have, however, was Antoine Dupont. No fly-half? No problem. Earlier in the week their head coach, Fabien Galthié, had dismissed the idea that he and his opposite number, Rassie Erasmus, were playing mindgames with each other as “comic-book stuff”. Turns out this was just another bluff. Galthié had said Dupont was going to start at fly-half and, sure, he wore No 10 on his back, but he played the game in his usual position. It was his understudy Maxime Lucu who switched positions to play first receiver.
